slides.title: Problems Every Operating System Must Solve
slides.body:
Standard Coordination Scenarios
When processes share data and run at the same time
Their steps can interleave unpredictably
Without coordination, one update can overwrite another
A timing bug called a race condition
slides.notes: Let's begin by understanding one of the most fundamental challenges in operating systems. When multiple processes access the same data at the same time, the order in which their instructions execute is unpredictable because their execution can interleave. Without proper coordination, one process may overwrite the changes made by another, leading to a timing-related error known as a race condition.

slides.title: Problems Every Operating System Must Solve
slides.body:
Standard Coordination Scenarios
A few standard problems capture the main coordination challenges. Each has a known semaphore solution — so recognising the pattern means the fix is already known
slides.notes: Let's begin with a common situation in an operating system. Imagine two processes trying to modify the same piece of data at nearly the same time. Since the operating system decides when each process gets the CPU, their instructions can execute in different orders every time. If this access isn't coordinated properly, one process can unknowingly overwrite the other's work. This kind of timing-dependent error is known as a race condition.

slides.title: Problems Every Operating System Must Solve
slides.body:
Classic Synchronization Problems
Coordinating a limited shared buffer (print queues, streaming)
Producer–Consumer
A Producer–Consumer variation with a barber and a bounded waiting room
Sleeping Barber
Many readers at once, but exclusive writes (databases, files)
Readers–Writers
Sharing resources safely without deadlock
Dining Philosophers
slides.notes: Before diving into the solutions, let's look at four classic synchronization problems that appear throughout operating systems.Producer–Consumer focuses on managing a limited shared buffer, Sleeping Barber extends that idea with a bounded waiting room, Readers–Writers balances concurrent reads with exclusive writes, and Dining Philosophers explores how processes can share resources safely while avoiding deadlock.

slides.title: Problems Every Operating System Must Solve
slides.body: Analogy
slides.notes: Think of these synchronization problems like learning recipes in cooking. Once a chef understands a few standard recipes, the same techniques can be applied to many different dishes. Similarly, when we master these classic Operating System synchronization problems, we begin to recognize the same coordination patterns in many real-world process communication and synchronization scenarios.

slides.title: Producer–Consumer Problem
slides.body: Producer–Consumer Problem
slides.notes: Now we will learn about the Producer – Consumer Problem

slides.title: Two Processes Sharing One Buffer
slides.body:
Producer–Consumer Problem
Two processes share one fixed-size buffer of n slots
 n slots
slides.notes: Let's start with the Producer–Consumer Problem. Here, two processes interact through a single fixed-size buffer containing n slots. One process is responsible for producing data and placing it into the buffer, while the other process consumes that data from the same buffer. Because both processes access the shared buffer, their actions must be carefully coordinated to ensure the buffer is used correctly.

slides.title: Producer – Consumer Problem
slides.body:
Bounded-Buffer Challenge
The producer creates items and puts them in
The buffer smooths out their different speeds
The consumer takes items out
slides.notes: Now, let's understand how the shared buffer is used. The producer keeps generating new items and places them into the buffer, while the consumer removes those items for processing. Since these two processes may not work at the same speed, the buffer acts as an intermediate storage area, allowing each process to continue at its own pace without requiring both to operate at exactly the same rate.

slides.title: Producer – Consumer Problem
slides.body:
Bounded-Buffer Challenge
Because the buffer is limited, a correct solution must guarantee three things:
No overflow
The producer waits when the buffer is full
No underflow
The consumer waits when the buffer is empty
Mutual exclusion
Only one process touches the buffer at any instant
Three separate requirements — which is why the solution needs three semaphores
slides.notes: Since the buffer has limited capacity, synchronization has to handle three different situations. It should prevent overflow by stopping the producer from adding more items when the buffer is full. It should also avoid underflow by making the consumer wait when no items are available. Along with this, mutual exclusion ensures that both processes don't access the shared buffer at the same time. These independent requirements are why the solution uses three semaphores.

slides.title: Producer – Consumer Problem
slides.body:
Analogy
Belt full
Belt empty
slides.notes: Imagine a conveyor belt with a fixed number of slots. The worker placing boxes is the Producer, and the worker removing them is the Consumer. If the belt is full, the Producer must wait. If it is empty, the Consumer waits. They also avoid accessing the same slot at the same time, just as processes use synchronization to safely share a buffer.

slides.title: Three Semaphores Working Together
slides.body:
Using wait() & signal()
Each requirement gets its own semaphore:
slides.notes: To satisfy these three requirements, the solution uses three semaphores, each with a specific responsibility. mutex is a binary semaphore initialized to 1, ensuring mutual exclusion while accessing the buffer. empty is a counting semaphore initialized to n, representing the available buffer slots. Finally, full is another counting semaphore initialized to 0, keeping track of how many slots currently contain data.
tables: Binary, mutual exclusion while accessing the buffer
Counting, number of empty slots (starts at buffer size n)
Counting, number of filled slots (starts at 0)

slides.title: Three Semaphores Working Together
slides.body:
The two counters mirror each other: producing turns an empty slot into a full one
Consuming does the reverse. When a counter reaches 0, wait() blocks the process automatically
Using wait() & signal()
slides.notes: Let's see how these semaphores work together. Every time the producer adds an item, one empty slot becomes full. Similarly, when the consumer removes an item, a full slot becomes empty again. If either counter reaches 0, calling wait() automatically blocks the corresponding process until the required resource becomes available

slides.title: How wait() & signal() Coordinate the Buffer
slides.notes: Let's understand how the producer coordinates using wait() and signal(). First, the producer creates an item. It then calls wait(empty) to ensure there is a free slot in the buffer. Next, wait(mutex) locks the buffer so only one process can access it. After adding the item, signal(mutex) unlocks the buffer, and signal(full) indicates that one more buffer slot is now filled.

slides.title: Three Semaphores Working Together
slides.notes: Now let's see how the consumer uses the three semaphores. It first calls wait(full) to ensure that an item is available in the buffer. Then, wait(mutex) locks the buffer before removing the item. After the item is removed, signal(mutex) unlocks the buffer, and signal(empty) indicates that one more buffer slot has become free.Finally, the consumer processes the removed item.

slides.title: Three Semaphores Working Together
slides.body:
Correct Semaphore Sequence
Order matters: check the count (empty/full) before locking (mutex) 
Reversing it, locking first, then finding no slot, freezes the process while it holds the lock.
slides.notes: Another important aspect is the order in which the semaphores are used. A process should first check the required resource using empty or full, and only then acquire mutex. If it locks mutex first and later discovers that no slot is available, it remains blocked while still holding the lock. This prevents other processes from making progress .

slides.title: Three Semaphores Working Together
slides.body:
Analogy
Total - 10 Parking Lots. Red color are filled lots, and Green are available lots
slides.notes: Think of this as a parking lot with a single entrance gate. The empty semaphore tracks how many parking spaces are available, while the full semaphore tracks how many are occupied. Before entering, a car checks whether a free space exists. The mutex semaphore acts as the entrance gate, allowing only one car to enter or exit at a time. This is exactly how the Producer and Consumer coordinate safe access to the shared buffer.

slides.title: A Variation of Producer - Consumer
slides.body:
Sleeping Barber Problem
A barber shop has:
When there are no customers, the barber sleeps
Fixed Number of Chairs
One Barber Chair
One Barber
slides.notes: Sleeping Barber Problem is modeled around a barber shop. The setup includes one barber, one barber chair, and a fixed number of waiting chairs for customers. If no customers are present, the barber sleeps, remaining idle until a new customer arrives.

slides.title: Sleeping Barber Problem
slides.body:
Producer–Consumer in Action
This models producers (customers) and a consumer (the barber) sharing a limited waiting room — the same pattern as Producer–Consumer
When a customer arrives:
If a chair is free, the customer sits and waits (and wakes the barber if he is asleep)
If the waiting room is full, the customer leaves
slides.notes: Now let's see why this is considered a Producer–Consumer variation. Whenever a customer arrives, the first step is to check whether a waiting chair is available. If there is space, the customer waits for service and wakes the barber if necessary. Otherwise, the customer leaves because the waiting room has reached its capacity. Here, the customers act as the producers, the barber acts as the consumer, and the waiting room behaves like a limited shared buffer.

slides.title: A Variation of Producer - Consumer
slides.body:
Using Three Semaphores
Three semaphores are used:
slides.notes: Just like the Producer–Consumer problem, the Sleeping Barber solution also relies on three semaphores, with each serving a different purpose. customers is initialized to 0 and keeps track of waiting customers. barber, also initialized to 0, is used to signal when the barber is ready to serve. Finally, mutex, initialized to 1, protects the shared count of free waiting chairs, ensuring it is updated safely.
tables: Signals whether the barber is ready
Protects the count of free waiting chairs

slides.title: A Variation of Producer - Consumer
slides.notes: Let's understand the barber's workflow. The barber first calls wait(customers) and sleeps until a customer arrives. Then, wait(mutex) locks the waiting-room data so it can be updated safely. The waiting count is decremented as one customer leaves the queue, signal(barber) notifies the customer that the barber is ready, and signal(mutex) unlocks the waiting-room. Finally, the barber starts cutting the customer's hair.

slides.title: A Variation of Producer - Consumer
slides.notes: Now let's look at the customer's workflow. The customer first calls wait(mutex) to safely access the waiting-room count. If a chair is available, the waiting count is incremented, signal(customers) wakes the barber, and signal(mutex) unlocks the waiting room. The customer then calls wait(barber) and waits until the barber is ready before getting a haircut. If no chair is available, the customer simply releases the mutex and leaves the shop.

slides.title: Readers–Writers Problem
slides.body: Readers–Writers Problem
slides.notes: Next we will be learning about the Readers – Writers Problem

slides.title: Many Readers, One Writer
slides.body:
Readers–Writers Problem
A shared resource, is used by many processes
The key insight: reading is safe together, but writing is not
Readers only view the data; writers change it. The goal is maximum concurrency without inconsistency
Process 1
Database
Process 1
File
Or
slides.notes: Here, multiple processes share a common resource such as a database or a file. Since readers only observe the data, they can access it simultaneously without causing issues. However, writers modify the shared resource, so their access must be carefully controlled. The objective is to achieve maximum concurrency while keeping the data consistent.

slides.title: Many Readers, One Writer
slides.body:
The Rules
Readers may read together — concurrent reading is always safe
A writer needs exclusive access — no reader or other writer active while it writes
Reading and writing must never overlap — this protects consistency
slides.notes: To satisfy the Readers–Writers Problem, a few rules must always be followed. 1 Multiple readers are allowed to access the shared resource at the same time because they don't change its contents. 2 A writer, however, requires exclusive access, meaning no other reader or writer can use the resource during an update. 3 Keeping reading and writing separate in this way ensures the shared data remains consistent.

slides.title: Readers–Writers Problem
slides.body: Analogy
slides.notes: Think of a public notice board. Many people can read it at the same time without causing any issues. However, when someone needs to write or update the board, everyone else must wait until the update is complete. In the same way, in the Readers–Writers Problem, multiple readers can access shared data together, but a writer requires exclusive access to maintain data consistency.

slides.title: Key Variables
slides.body:
Readers–Writers Solution
The solution uses one counter and two semaphores:
slides.notes: To enforce these rules, the solution maintains one counter and two semaphores, each with a specific role. read_count, initialized to 0, keeps track of how many readers are currently accessing the shared resource. Since multiple readers can update this counter, mutex protects it from concurrent modification. The rw_mutex semaphore provides exclusive access to a writer, ensuring that no writer can proceed while readers are active.
tables: Gives a writer exclusive access; blocks writers while readers are active
How many readers are currently reading

slides.title: The read_count Logic
slides.body:
How It Works?
First reader
locks rw_mutex, shutting writers out
Extra readers
just increase read_count and read freely
Last reader
(count back to 0) releases rw_mutex, letting a writer in
Mutex
protects read_count so two readers never update it at once
slides.notes: The idea behind read_count is to coordinate readers without blocking each one individually. 1 The first reader acquires rw_mutex, preventing any writer from entering. 2 As more readers arrive, they simply increment read_count and continue reading together. 3 When the last reader finishes and read_count returns to 0, it releases rw_mutex, allowing a waiting writer to proceed.4 Throughout this process, mutex protects read_count so only one reader updates it at a time.

slides.title: Writer Logic
slides.notes: Let's understand the writer's workflow. The writer first calls wait(rw_mutex) to request exclusive access to the shared resource. Once the semaphore is acquired, it performs the writing operation. After completing the update, the writer calls signal(rw_mutex) to release the resource, allowing other readers or writers to access it.

slides.title: Reader Logic
slides.notes: Now let's understand the reader's workflow. The reader first locks mutex and increments read_count. If it is the first reader, it calls wait(rw_mutex) to block writers. After releasing mutex, it performs the reading operation. Once finished, it locks mutex again, decrements read_count, and if it is the last reader, it calls signal(rw_mutex) to allow writers to proceed. Finally, it releases mutex.

slides.title: Writer Starvation
slides.body:
Trade-Off Of Reader Preference
While readers keep arriving, read_count never hits 0, so a writer can wait a long time
This is writer starvation — read-heavy systems accept it; others use writer-priority variants
slides.notes: One limitation of the reader-preference approach is writer starvation. If new readers keep arriving, read_count may never return to 0, preventing a waiting writer from acquiring rw_mutex. As a result, the writer can be delayed indefinitely. While this trade-off is acceptable in read-heavy systems, other implementations use writer-priority policies to reduce or eliminate starvation.

slides.title: The read_count Variable
slides.body: Analogy
slides.notes: Think of the shared data as a room that readers can enter. The first reader locks the room to prevent any writer from entering. As more readers arrive or leave, only the read_count is updated. When the last reader exits, it unlocks the room, allowing a writer to access the shared resource.

slides.title: Dining Philosophers Problem
slides.body: Dining Philosophers Problem
slides.notes: Next we will be learning about the Dining Philosophers Problem

slides.title: Five Philosophers, Five Chopsticks
slides.body:
Classic Illustration of Deadlock
They alternate between thinking and eating
There is one chopstick between each pair of neighbouring philosophers, making five chopsticks in total
To eat, a philosopher must pick up both neighbouring chopsticks.
After eating, the philosopher puts both chopsticks down and goes back to thinking
Five philosophers sit around a round table.
slides.notes: The final classic synchronization problem is the Dining Philosophers problem. Imagine five philosophers sitting around a circular table, alternating between thinking and eating. There are five chopsticks, with one placed between each neighbouring pair of philosophers. Before a philosopher can eat, both neighbouring chopsticks must be picked up. Once the meal is finished, both chopsticks are placed back on the table, and the philosopher returns to thinking.

slides.title: Shared Resource Coordination
slides.body:
Dining Philosophers Problem
This models processes that each need more than one shared resource at the same time
Basic approach — each chopstick is a semaphore (initialised to 1). A philosopher takes the left, then the right, eats, then puts both down:
slides.notes: This problem represents a situation where a process needs more than one shared resource to complete its work. In the Dining Philosophers Problem, each chopstick is treated as a semaphore initialized to 1, meaning only one philosopher can hold it at a time. Following the basic approach, a philosopher first picks up the left chopstick, then the right one, eats, and finally releases both chopsticks for others to use.

slides.title: Five Philosophers, Five Chopsticks
slides.notes: Let's understand the philosopher's workflow. Each philosopher first calls wait(chopstick[i]) to pick up the left chopstick, followed by wait(chopstick[(i + 1) mod 5]) to pick up the right one. After acquiring both chopsticks, the philosopher eats and then releases them using the two signal() calls before thinking again. Although this logic ensures that no two philosophers use the same chopstick at the same time, it can still lead to a situation where all philosophers end up waiting, preventing anyone from eating.

slides.title: Dining Philosophers Problem
slides.body: Analogy
slides.notes: Think of two people working at a craft table. One needs the scissors, and the other needs the glue stick, but each task requires both items. If each person picks up one item and waits for the other, neither can continue. This is exactly what happens in the Dining Philosophers Problem, where each process holds one resource while waiting for another,

slides.title: Dining Philosophers Deadlock
slides.body:
When Everyone Waits Forever
This is a deadlock
If all five pick up their left chopstick at the same moment, every chopstick is held and each waits forever for the right one. Nobody proceeds
P2
P1
P1
P3
P4
P5
slides.notes: Now let's see where the problem occurs. Imagine all five philosophers pick up their left chopstick at the same time. Each philosopher now holds one chopstick but is waiting for the right chopstick, which is already held by a neighbour. As a result, no one can continue, no one releases the chopstick they already have, and the entire system comes to a standstill.This situation is called a deadlock.

slides.title: Breaking the Circular Wait
slides.body:
The Lesson
Locking each resource is not enough
The order in which locks are taken can still trap the system
slides.notes: The key takeaway from this example is that simply locking every shared resource does not guarantee a correct solution. Even if each resource is protected, acquiring the locks in an inappropriate order can create a circular wait, where every process is waiting for another to release a resource. Avoiding this situation is essential to prevent deadlock.

slides.title: Breaking the Circular Wait
slides.body:
Three Standard Solutions
Three standard fixes break the circle:
slides.notes: To prevent this circular wait, three standard approaches are commonly used. One limits the system to at most four philosophers at a time. Another follows the pick up both or neither rule, so a philosopher never waits while holding a single chopstick. The third uses asymmetric ordering, where odd and even philosophers pick up the chopsticks in different orders, preventing deadlock.
tables: Allow at most 4 at the table
With four competing for five chopsticks, at least one can always obtain both, so the system never fully locks up
A philosopher takes both chopsticks together only if both are free, so it never holds one while waiting
Odd philosophers pick up the left chopstick first, even philosophers the right first, so the circular wait never forms

slides.title: Breaking the Circular Wait
slides.body:
Analogy
1
2
3
slides.notes: Imagine a table with five seats but only four people dining. Because one seat remains empty, there is always a spare chopstick available, allowing at least one person to eat and then release both chopsticks. Similarly, by allowing at most four philosophers, the Dining Philosophers Problem avoids circular wait and prevents deadlock.

slides.title: Inter-Process Communication (IPC)
slides.body: Inter-Process Communication (IPC)
slides.notes: Now we will learn about the Inter-Process Communication (IPC)

slides.title: Why Processes Need to Communicate
slides.body:
Inter-Process Communication (IPC)
For safety, the OS keeps each process in its own private memory
One process cannot read another's memory directly. This isolation stops a faulty program from corrupting others.
slides.notes: So far, we've looked at processes coordinating their execution. But sometimes, processes also need to exchange information. By default, the operating system gives every process its own private memory, preventing one process from directly accessing another's memory. This isolation improves safety by ensuring that a faulty process cannot accidentally corrupt the data of other processes.

slides.title: Inter-Process Communication (IPC)
slides.body:
Safe Process Communication
IPC is the set of OS mechanisms that let processes share data and coordinate through safe, controlled channels
slides.notes: To enable this interaction, operating systems provide Inter-Process Communication (IPC). Rather than allowing processes to access each other's memory directly, IPC offers safe, controlled channels through which they can exchange data and coordinate their activities securely.

slides.title: How Processes Talk to Each Other
slides.body:
Why Processes Need IPC:
Data sharing
Cooperating processes must pass information
Modularity
A large task splits into smaller processes
Coordination
One process signals another (e.g., 'data is ready')
Speed
Separate processes work in parallel and combine results
slides.notes: Processes communicate through IPC for several reasons.1  They use it for data sharing, allowing cooperating processes to exchange information. 2 It also supports modularity by dividing a large task into smaller processes. 3 Through coordination, one process can notify another when an event, such as "data is ready," occurs. 4 Finally, speed improves because multiple processes can execute in parallel and later combine their results.

slides.title: How Processes Talk to Each Other
slides.body: Analogy
slides.notes: Think of processes as people working in separate rooms. Since they cannot directly access each other's space, they communicate through safe methods, such as passing notes under the door or sharing a whiteboard through a window. Similarly, processes use IPC mechanisms like Message Passing and Shared Memory to exchange information while maintaining isolation and safety.

slides.title: Shared Memory IPC
slides.body:
Direct Memory Sharing
Shared Memory — The OS gives two processes a common memory region; they exchange data by reading and writing it directly
Very fast, but they must add their own synchronization (e.g., a semaphore) or hit race conditions
common memory region
OS
slides.notes: One IPC method is Shared Memory. Here, the operating system creates a common memory region that both processes can access, allowing them to exchange data by reading and writing directly. Since this method is very fast, the processes must use synchronization, such as a semaphore, to avoid race conditions.

slides.title: Message Passing
slides.body:
Message Passing, processes never share memory; they exchange messages using send() and receive(). Slower, since the OS handles each message, but safer, and it works across different machines
Exchanging Messages Safely

slides.notes:
Another IPC method is Message Passing. Unlike Shared Memory, processes never share memory directly. Instead, they communicate using send() and receive(), with the kernel handling every message. Although this is slower, it is safer and also supports communication between processes running on different machines.

This diagram illustrates the flow of Message Passing. First, Process A sends a message to the kernel using send(). The operating system then delivers that message to Process B, which receives it using receive(). Because every message passes through the kernel, communication is safer, although it is slightly slower than Shared Memory.

slides.title: Shared vs Message
slides.body: Key Differences
tables: Fast, no OS help per access
Same machine or across a network

slides.title: Design Choices
slides.body:
Message Passing
Message passing has three design choices
slides.notes: When designing a Message Passing system, the operating system makes three important design choices. 1 Naming decides whether communication is direct between processes or indirect through a shared mailbox. 2 Synchronization determines whether communication is blocking or non-blocking. 3 Finally, buffering defines whether the communication channel has zero, bounded, or unbounded capacity.

slides.title: Shared Memory and Message Passing
slides.body:
Analogy
Shared memory
Message passing
slides.notes: Think of Shared Memory as a shared whiteboard. It's very fast, but processes need synchronization, such as a semaphore, to avoid conflicts. Message Passing is like sending letters—slower, but safer because processes never access the same memory directly.

slides.title: IPC Mechanisms
slides.body:
Choosing the Right Tool
The two models are realised through several concrete mechanisms, each suited to a different situation
slides.notes: So far, we've discussed the two IPC models. In practice, these are implemented using different IPC mechanisms, each designed for specific communication needs. The right mechanism depends on factors such as speed, safety, and the way processes need to exchange information.

slides.title: IPC Mechanisms
slides.body: Common Communication Tools
slides.notes: The operating system provides several IPC mechanisms, each suited to different situations. 1 & 2 Pipes and Named Pipes (FIFO) transfer data between processes,3 Message Queues exchange messages through the OS, 4 Shared Memory offers the fastest communication but requires a 5 semaphore for synchronization,6 Signals send simple event notifications, 7 and Sockets enable communication both within a system and across networks.
tables: A one-way channel between related processes, such as a parent and child
Like a pipe but named in the file system, so unrelated processes can use it
An OS-managed list of messages; processes post and retrieve them, often by priority
A common region mapped into several processes; fastest, but needs a semaphore
Synchronizes access between processes rather than carrying bulk data
A short asynchronous notification, e.g. to tell a process an event occurred
A two-way endpoint that works on one machine or across a network

slides.title: Message Communication
slides.body:
Synchronous vs Asynchronous
Synchronous vs asynchronous communication:
Synchronous (blocking)
  Asynchronous (non-blocking)
The sender waits until the message is received. Like a phone call
The sender continues immediately; the receiver reads later. Like a letter
slides.notes: Message communication can be either synchronous or asynchronous. In synchronous (blocking) communication, the sender waits until the message is received, much like a phone call. In asynchronous (non-blocking) communication, the sender continues immediately, and the receiver reads the message later, similar to sending a letter.

slides.title: IPC in Real Life
slides.body: Analogy
slides.notes: Analogy: Choosing an IPC mechanism is like choosing how to send something: a quick note to the person next to you, a shared noticeboard, a posted parcel, or a phone line to another city.

slides.title: Pipes — A Simple Channel Between Processes
slides.body:
Introduction
A pipe is one of the oldest and simplest IPC mechanisms: 
A channel where one process writes data at one end and another reads it from the other end, in first-in-first-out order
There are two kinds
Ordinary (anonymous) pipe
Named pipe (FIFO)
Reads
Writes
slides.notes: One of the simplest IPC mechanisms is a Pipe. It acts as a communication channel where one process writes data and another process reads it in First-In-First-Out (FIFO) order. Pipes are of two types: Ordinary (anonymous) pipes and Named pipes (FIFO), each used in different communication scenarios.

slides.title: Pipes — A Simple Channel Between Processes
slides.body:
Ordinary (anonymous) Pipe
Carries data one way only — one end for writing, one end for reading. (Two-way needs two pipes.)
Works only between related processes — typically a parent and the child it creates, because the child inherits the pipe when it is forked
It is temporary: the pipe exists only while the processes are running and disappears once they finish
Ordinary Pipes
slides.notes: An Ordinary (anonymous) Pipe provides one-way communication, where one process writes and the other reads. If two-way communication is needed, two pipes are required. It works only between related processes, such as a parent and child, because the child inherits the pipe during fork(). Since it is temporary, the pipe is removed once the processes terminate.

slides.title: Pipes — A Simple Channel Between Processes
slides.body:
Has a name in the file system, so it exists independently of any process
Because it has a name, unrelated processes (not just parent-child) can use it to communicate.
It persists until explicitly deleted and typically provides one-way communication; two-way communication requires two FIFOs
Named Pipes (FIFOs)
Named Pipe (FIFO):
slides.notes: Unlike an Ordinary Pipe, a Named Pipe (FIFO) is identified by a name in the file system, so the communicating processes do not have to be related. Since it remains available until it is explicitly deleted, different processes can connect to it whenever needed. Like an ordinary pipe, two FIFOs are required if communication is needed in both directions.

slides.title: Ordinary Pipes and Named Pipes (FIFOs)
slides.body:
Analogy
Ordinary pipe
Named pipe
slides.notes: Think of an Ordinary Pipe as a private pipeline between a parent and child process. A Named Pipe (FIFO) is like a public water tap—any process that knows its name can use it, even if the processes are unrelated.
